title: Producers, queue, consumers — and back pressure
description: A queue decouples the rate work arrives from the rate it is done. That is its value and also its danger: an unbounded buffer hides a problem until it is a large one.

steps.text: A request arrives that triggers slow work — a video to transcode, a report to build, an email to send.
The web server writes a durable job and returns immediately. The user gets a fast response; the work has been accepted, not completed.
Workers pull jobs at whatever rate they can sustain. Producers and consumers now scale, deploy and fail independently — the real payoff, more than the latency win.
The result is written. The client learns about it by polling a status endpoint, a webhook, or a push — because the original request is long gone.
Producers keep publishing at the arrival rate. Nothing upstream knows or cares that consumers are struggling.
Consumers drain more slowly than jobs arrive. The queue grows. Time-through-queue climbs from milliseconds toward hours, and by the time anyone notices, the backlog itself takes hours to clear.

Back pressure is the fix: bound the queue and reject or slow producers when it is full. The alternative is not 'no back pressure' — it is an unbounded buffer and a much worse failure later. Alert on queue depth trend; it is the earliest signal you get.
A malformed job fails, is redelivered, and fails again — consuming a worker each time and blocking anything behind it.

After a bounded number of attempts it moves to a dead-letter queue: out of the way, still preserved for inspection and replay once fixed. A growing DLQ is one of the highest-signal alerts in the system.
